title: Twins Reared Apart
text:
In 1979, Thomas Bouchard at the University of Minnesota read a newspaper story about identical twin brothers in Ohio, both named Jim, who had been adopted into different families as babies and had just met again at 39. He invited them to Minneapolis for testing, and soon the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart was under way.

Over the following years, the team brought more than a hundred sets of twins and triplets who had been raised apart, from many countries, to Minneapolis for about a week of intensive testing. They underwent medical exams, intelligence tests, personality questionnaires and long interviews about their lives and interests. Identical twins, who share all their genes, could be compared with fraternal twins, who share about half.

In a 1990 paper in Science, Bouchard, David Lykken, Matt McGue, Nancy Segal and Auke Tellegen reported that identical twins raised in different homes were about as similar as identical twins raised together on many measures of personality, interests and social attitudes. On intelligence, they estimated that about 70 percent of the variation in their sample was associated with genetic differences.

The study was a major force in convincing psychologists that genes play a substantial role in human differences.
lesson: Children are not blank slates, and much of who they are comes with them. Parents shape a child, but they work with a nature that is already there.
people: Thomas Bouchard, David Lykken, Matt McGue, Nancy Segal, Auke Tellegen
source: Bouchard, T. J., Lykken, D. T., McGue, M., Segal, N. L., and Tellegen, A. (1990). Sources of human psychological differences: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart. Science, 250(4978), 223-228.
caveat: Many twins had some contact before testing and were raised in fairly similar homes, and heritability estimates apply to a population, not to any individual.
